meta.name: Run parallel webhook services with HTTP Request fan-out

name: Run Tasks in Parallel with HTTP Request Fan-Out and Webhooks

assignments.name: ranInParallel
assignments.value: ={{ Math.max(...$('HTTP Request').all().map(i => new Date(i.json.startedAt).getTime())) < Math.min(...$('HTTP Request').all().map(i => new Date(i.json.endAt).getTime())) }}

assignments.name: startGapSeconds
assignments.value: ={{ (Math.max(...$('HTTP Request').all().map(i => new Date(i.json.startedAt).getTime())) - Math.min(...$('HTTP Request').all().map(i => new Date(i.json.startedAt).getTime()))) / 1000 }}

assignments.name: totalWallSeconds
assignments.value: ={{ (Math.max(...$('HTTP Request').all().map(i => new Date(i.json.endAt).getTime())) - Math.min(...$('HTTP Request').all().map(i => new Date(i.json.startedAt).getTime()))) / 1000 }}

assignments.name: sumOfDurations
assignments.value: ={{ $('HTTP Request').all().reduce((a, i) => a + (new Date(i.json.endAt).getTime() - new Date(i.json.startedAt).getTime()), 0) / 1000 }}

assignments.name: savedSeconds
assignments.value: ={{ $('HTTP Request').all().reduce((a, i) => a + (new Date(i.json.endAt).getTime() - new Date(i.json.startedAt).getTime()), 0) / 1000 - (Math.max(...$('HTTP Request').all().map(i => new Date(i.json.endAt).getTime())) - Math.min(...$('HTTP Request').all().map(i => new Date(i.json.startedAt).getTime()))) / 1000 }}

assignments.name: finishOrder
assignments.value: ={{ [...$('HTTP Request').all()].sort((a, b) => new Date(a.json.endAt).getTime() - new Date(b.json.endAt).getTime()).map(i => i.json.service) }}

assignments.name: runs
assignments.value: ={{ $('HTTP Request').all().map(i => ({ service: i.json.service, executionId: i.json.executionId, durationSeconds: (new Date(i.json.endAt).getTime() - new Date(i.json.startedAt).getTime()) / 1000, startedAt: i.json.startedAt, endAt: i.json.endAt })) }}

parameters.content:
## 🔧 Simulated services

Each branch = an independent execution triggered by the fan-out. The Wait node (7s / 2s / 13s) stands in for real work, swap it for an LLM call, API request, or anything.

The response is a deliberate whitelist: `{service, startedAt, endAt, executionId}` Keep this contract when you customize, the proof node above reads it.

### 💡Reading the results

The output provides several independent indicators of how the tasks were executed:

- **`ranInParallel`** — `true` when every task's `[start, end]` interval overlaps with the others. With sequential execution, the next request could not start until the previous request had completed, so this overlap would not occur.

- **`totalWallSeconds` vs `sumOfDurations`** — the total elapsed time is close to the duration of the slowest task rather than the sum of all task durations. `savedSeconds` shows the time saved by running them concurrently.

- **The three orderings** — `itemOrder`, `arrivalOrder`, and `finishOrder` show different stages of the process:
  - `itemOrder` — the order of the original input items sent by the parent workflow.
  - `arrivalOrder` — the order in which the webhook executions reached the n8n server.
  - `finishOrder` — the order in which the individual tasks completed.

In a typical run, these orders can differ. For example, requests dispatched as 1-2-3 may arrive as 3-2-1 because they are already in flight at the same time, while the completion order reflects the actual workload duration.

The HTTP Request node can still return the results in the original item order because responses are re-paired by item index.

Every row in `runs` also contains its `executionId`, allowing each individual webhook execution to be inspected directly in n8n's Executions list.

## ⚡ Orchestrator: fan out & verify

Merge turns three branches into three items → one HTTP Request dispatches them all at once → Prove Parallel reads the receipts.

## Run Tasks in Parallel with HTTP Request Fan-Out and Webhooks

Fan out any number of tasks concurrently from one HTTP Request node, with timestamps, execution IDs, and an automated report to verify how they ran.

### Who's it for

Builders who need several independent tasks, such as API calls, model queries, scraping jobs, or other workloads, to run at the same time instead of one after another.

This template is also useful if you want to inspect and verify the actual execution behavior rather than simply assuming that a workflow is running in parallel.

### What it does

n8n's engine runs one node at a time, so parallel-looking branches do not execute concurrently. The concurrency in this template comes from inside a single node: the HTTP Request node starts a request for every input item without waiting for the previous response, so all requests can be in flight at the same time. Most other nodes process items one by one, so this is a behavior of the HTTP Request node, not of items in general.

The Batching option controls how many requests are started at once. Setting `Items per Batch` to `-1` sends all items without batching, allowing all requests to be started concurrently. (Note that `0` is treated as `1`, so `-1` is the only value that fully disables batching.)

Each input item contains the URL of a webhook on the same n8n instance, and every incoming webhook call starts its own independent execution. The parent workflow keeps the HTTP connections open while those executions run. When they finish, their responses are re-paired with the original items by index, so the results remain in a predictable order regardless of which task finishes first.

Compared with the callback pattern using **Execute Workflow** with "Wait for Sub-workflow" disabled, `$execution.resumeUrl`, and resumable Wait nodes, this approach requires no resume URLs, retry loops, or routing logic. Request and response pairing is handled natively by the HTTP Request node.

The trade-off is that the parent workflow holds the HTTP connections open for the duration of the tasks, so this approach is best suited to workloads that complete in seconds or a few minutes. For very long-running jobs, a callback-based pattern is generally more appropriate.

### How it works

1. Three Set nodes define the "services". Each contains a webhook URL and a payload.
2. A Merge node with 3 inputs in **Append** mode combines them into a single stream of three items.
3. A single **HTTP Request** node with batching disabled (`Items per Batch: -1`) sends all three POST requests concurrently.
4. Each webhook branch records `startedAt`, simulates work with a Wait node (7s / 2s / 13s), and returns a minimal response containing `{service, startedAt, endAt, executionId}`.
5. A **Prove Parallel** node, a Set node with **Execute Once** enabled that reads `$('HTTP Request').all()`, analyzes the results and generates the concurrency report without using a Code node.

### Setup

1. Replace `YOUR-N8N-URL` in the three service nodes with your instance's base URL. 
2. **Activate** the workflow. Production `/webhook/` paths only exist while the workflow is active.
3. Click **Execute**. You'll see four executions: the manual parent execution plus three webhook executions. Their execution IDs appear in the report.

### How to customize: use it as a blueprint

This template is a pattern, not a finished workflow, and its two halves are independently reusable:

- **The orchestrator half** (Set nodes → Merge → HTTP Request → Prove Parallel) can be grafted into any existing workflow that needs a fan-out step. Replace the Set nodes with whatever produces your list of targets — one item per task, each carrying a `link` and `payload` — and everything downstream of the HTTP Request node receives the collected results in item order.
- **The service half** (Webhook → work → Respond) is the skeleton of a reusable internal micro-service. Swap the Wait node for real work — an LLM call, an API request, a scrape — and any workflow on your instance can then call it, in parallel or on its own. Keeping the `{service, startedAt, endAt, executionId}` response contract costs nothing and gives every caller latency telemetry plus a direct link to the execution for debugging.
- To add a service: copy one webhook branch, add one Set node in the orchestrator, and increase the Merge node's Number of Inputs.
- **Prove Parallel** is demo instrumentation. Delete it in production, or keep it: `durationSeconds` per service is exactly the per-task latency you would want to log anyway.

When the tasks become real, set an explicit **Timeout** in the HTTP Request node sized to your slowest task.
